rv.q: Daniel Raggett's staging makes the most of Hare's witty one-liners without sacrificing the essential bleakness of this story.

Hare has great fun, too, with the bumbling student Anson (fluently played by Roman Asde) who falls under Maggie’s spell. Yes, the evening has its flaws. I never quite believed in Maggie’s old flame, songwriter Arthur (the fine Michael Fox), who often whiles away the time vamping on standards by the likes of Cole Porter.
In the end, Maggie’s screams ring out around the cloisters, the dreaming spires where acid dreams go to die.
This is sharp, funny, smile-inducing pleasure for rock-loving graduates of a certain vintage.
All very dated, but a spicy trip down memory lane.
Maybe that’s to do with the gloss of the production.
The show comes alive with every song.
Yet, the problems with Hare’s play persist.
Does it have anything of burning import to say to us in 2026? The awkward answer is a resounding 'No'
But as a complete production, it just doesn't work, and was probably never going to work.

Read our review of David Hare's play Teeth 'n' Smiles, now in performances at the Duke of York's Theatre to 6 June. It’s no wonder, really, why David Hare’s 1969-set play about a fading rock star drinking through the diminuendo of her demise is produced so infrequently.
Taylor is sensational as Maggie, full of self-loathing and fight in almost equal measure.

Each band and crew member contributes to the musical numbers with aplomb, but there is little time to develop their individual personas in the scenes between songs, resulting in mere outlandish and laddish stereotypes and a lack of depth to their characters.
Rebecca Lucy Taylor (aka Self Esteem) plays Maggie perfectly well as a prattling narcissistic nuisance but it’s a role that demands little depth or subtlety.
There's fun to be had in Daniel Raggett's production, stripping away distraction and funnelling all attention onto Maggie's slow-motion implosion.
What they seem unable to provide, however, is the energy, the power, the flash of a good rock band.
Energetic, sometimes entertaining, but ultimately held back by writing and structure that have not aged as well as its creators might hope.

There appears to be no character depth or development, no serious issues explored and little insight into a fragment of a drunken subculture that has no sense of the world in which it is supposed to exist.
Beyond that, this David Hare revival is toothless.
But a series of challenges dull the drama’s emotional rage.

cn.t: Mixed reviews for Hare's 1975 rock drama, now feeling dated despite Rebecca Lucy Taylor's incendiary performance as self-destructive singer Maggie. Critics praise her star turn but find the play itself an expletive-laden period piece that's lost its bite.
